proof:
# All stationary sections at a tetrahedral median-line point

This is an ordinary three-dimensional theorem. It covers every section
plane in its stated class, including full-rank balanced collections. It
is not the weighted stationary-section theorem for an arbitrary convex
body, nor for an arbitrary point of a tetrahedron, and implies no general
mixed-integer depth bound.

## 1. The theorem

Let T be any tetrahedron of volume V>0, with vertices v_0,...,v_3 and
barycentric coordinates xi_0,...,xi_3. Let y have barycentric coordinates

    lambda=(a,b,b,b),    a>0, b>0, a+3b=1.

Thus y is any interior point of a vertex-to-opposite-face median. Let
u_i be finitely many unit vectors, and suppose each plane through y
normal to u_i cuts T in a section Q_i whose two-dimensional centroid is
y. Put

    S_i=area(Q_i),
    p_i=vol(T intersect {x:u_i.(x-y)>=0})/V.

If theta_i>=0, sum theta_i=1, and

    sum_i theta_i S_i u_i=0,

then

    sum_i theta_i p_i >= 27/64.                         (1)

Equality holds exactly when a=b=1/4 and, after discarding zero weights
and grouping repeated caps, the four caps are the canonical vertex caps
{xi_j>=1/4}, each with weight 1/4. In particular positive weight on a
quadrilateral section makes (1) strict.

All centroids and areas are Euclidean in their own affine planes. Every
section is a proper positive-area section because y is interior. The
proof uses raw gradients only multiplied by their exact coarea factors;
therefore its vector identities are unchanged by an invertible affine
change of the tetrahedron's coordinates. Explicitly, under x'=Lx+v,
the section vectors transform as `S'u'=|det L|L^(-T)(Su)`, while
`V'=|det L|V` and `g'-y'=L(g-y)`. Both the vector balance and every
scalar s_i below are therefore preserved.

## 2. A scalar correction suffices

Let g be the ordinary centroid of T, and put

    s_i=S_i u_i.(g-y)/V.

The vector balance implies sum theta_i s_i=0. Hence it suffices to find
one real number c such that every admitted oriented section satisfies

    p_i-c s_i >=27/64.                                  (2)

Reversing a section changes (p,s) to (1-p,-s), so a two-sided bound
27/64<=p-cs<=37/64 for one orientation proves (2) for both.

When a<=3/8 we use

    c=2b/(6b-1)>0.                                      (3)

Here 5/24<=b<1/3. The case a>3/8 will have only one unoriented section
and will be handled separately.

## 3. Every vertex-isolating section

A triangular proper section can be oriented toward a single vertex v_j.
This includes a plane containing one or two of the other vertices.
Write its three edge-intersection parameters from v_j as t_l, l!=j.
The section centroid has barycentric coordinates t_l/3 at l!=j.
Consequently it has centroid y exactly when t_l=3 lambda_l. This is
possible exactly when every lambda_l<=1/3 for l!=j, and its cap fraction is

    p_j=27 product_(l!=j) lambda_l.

A raw cap margin is

    m_j=3-sum_(l!=j) xi_l/lambda_l.

It vanishes at y, has value 3 at v_j, and its gradient is nonzero. The
cap is a pyramid of height 3/|grad m_j| over its section. Therefore

    S_j/(V |grad m_j|)=p_j,
    s_j=p_j[3-(1/4)sum_(l!=j)1/lambda_l].               (4)

This pyramid identity also proves the coarea normalization in all
endpoint cases without a transversality limit.

For lambda=(a,b,b,b), substitution of (3) and a+3b=1 gives the SAME
corrected value for every available vertex-side cap:

    p_j-c s_j=Q_V(b)=27b^3/[2(6b-1)].                   (5)

This covers j=0, always available, and j!=0 when a<=1/3. Directly,

    Q_V(b)-27/64
      =27(2b+1)(4b-1)^2/[64(6b-1)] >=0.                (6)

On [5/24,1/3], the derivative of Q_V has the sign of 4b-1, since

    Q_V'(b)=81b^2(4b-1)/[2(6b-1)^2].

Its maximum on that interval is attained at an endpoint, and

    Q_V(5/24)=125/256,    Q_V(1/3)=1/2.

Thus all vertex-side caps have corrected value in [27/64,1/2], and
their complements have corrected value at least 1/2. Equality at the
lower endpoint in (6) requires b=1/4.

## 4. Equal centroid coordinates force equal heights on one side

Every genuine quadrilateral section strictly separates two vertices
from the other two. Orient and relabel it so that its positive side
contains v_0,v_1 and its negative side contains v_2,v_3. We show that
its raw values at v_2 and v_3 must coincide. Only lambda_2=lambda_3=b<1/3
is used; no restriction a<=1/3 is imposed.

Here is the needed diagonal calculation, included to avoid an inverse
uniqueness assumption. Normalize the positive barycentric coordinates of
the quadrilateral's diagonal intersection as (x,y,z,w), with sum one.
Its plane has raw vertex values

    (1/x,1/y,-1/z,-1/w).

Indeed its four cyclic vertices are

    A=(x,0,z,0)/(x+z),    B=(x,0,0,w)/(x+w),
    C=(0,y,0,w)/(y+w),    D=(0,y,z,0)/(y+z),

and their diagonals both contain (x,y,z,w). Conversely any quadrilateral
section has such a positive diagonal point, and these endpoints and raw
values are thereby determined. Its centroid is (A+B+C+D-e)/3, where e
is the diagonal intersection: triangulating on one diagonal and weighting
the two triangle centroids by their areas proves this identity.

Set alpha=xy, beta=zw, and

    Delta=(x+z)(x+w)(y+z)(y+w)>0.

The resulting centroid formulas give

    3(lambda_2-lambda_3)
       =(z-w)[alpha-(alpha-beta)^2]/Delta.               (7)

They also show that lambda_2,lambda_3<=1/3 are respectively equivalent to

    (beta-alpha)z<=alpha,
    (beta-alpha)w<=alpha.                               (8)

The bracket in (7) is strictly positive under (8). If alpha>=beta,
then 0<=alpha-beta<alpha<1, so its square is less than alpha. If
beta>alpha and (beta-alpha)^2>=alpha, put Z=max(z,w)>=sqrt(beta).
Then (beta-alpha)Z>=sqrt(alpha beta)>alpha, contradicting (8).
Thus (7) and equality of the two centroid coordinates force z=w.
This proves the asserted equality of the two negative raw vertex values.

## 5. A complete conic parameterization of the quadrilateral planes

Scale the common negative vertex value to -1. The plane's raw margin
can then be written

    m=xi_0/A+xi_1/B-1,    0<A<1, 0<B<1.               (9)

The edge intercepts on the 0-to-negative edges are A, and those on the
1-to-negative edges are B. Parameterize the section by
xi_0=A(1-t), xi_1=Bt, 0<=t<=1, with the remaining coordinates sharing
1-A(1-t)-Bt. In affine section coordinates its area element is a fixed
positive constant times this last width times dt. Integration gives

    lambda_0=A(3-2A-B)/[3(2-A-B)],
    lambda_1=B(3-A-2B)/[3(2-A-B)],
    lambda_2=lambda_3=(1-lambda_0-lambda_1)/2.

The condition lambda_1=lambda_2 is therefore exactly

    A^2+2AB+3B^2-3A-6B+3=0.                             (10)

Every solution of (10) in the open unit square has the form

    A=3r^2/[2(r^2+2)],
    B=(r^2-2r+4)/[2(r^2+2)],    0<r<2.                 (11)

For completeness, the solution with B=1/2 is A=1/2 and corresponds
to r=1. Otherwise let h=(A-1/2)/(B-1/2). Substitution in (10), after
removing its known root (1/2,1/2), yields

    A=3(h+1)^2/[2(h^2+2h+3)],
    B=(h^2+4h+7)/[2(h^2+2h+3)].

The conditions A<1 and B<1 imply respectively -3<h<1 and |h|>1,
hence -3<h<-1. Set r=-h-1 to obtain (11). The converse follows by
substitution. Thus no branch or possible inverse multiplicity is lost.

The common centroid corresponding to (11) is

    a=r^2(4-r)/[4(r^2+2)],
    b=(r^3+8)/[12(r^2+2)].                             (12)

In particular every quadrilateral section in question has a<3/8.
Indeed this inequality is equivalent to

    2r^3-5r^2+6>0.

On [0,2] this polynomial decreases until r=5/3 and increases afterward;
its minimum is 37/27>0. This also proves that no quadrilateral section
exists at any median-line point with a>=3/8.

## 6. Exact quadrilateral cap and correction bounds

For the orientation m>=0 in (9), use the elementary barycentric density
6(1-xi_0-xi_1) on {xi_0,xi_1>=0, xi_0+xi_1<=1}. Its complement in T
projects to the triangle xi_0/A+xi_1/B<1. Integrating this affine density
on that triangle gives the cap fraction

    F=1-AB(3-A-B).

This can equivalently be verified by triangulating the tetrahedron; the
normalization follows because the integral of that density on the full
coordinate triangle is one. Moving the threshold m>=s for sufficiently
small s replaces A,B in the complementary triangle by (1+s)A,(1+s)B.
Its normalized coarea section factor is consequently

    S/(V |grad m|)=3AB(2-A-B).

The raw margin at the ordinary tetrahedral centroid is
(1/A+1/B)/4-1. Hence the scalar moment in Section 2 is exactly

    s=(3/4)(2-A-B)(A+B-4AB).                            (13)

Use (3), (11), and (12), and set h(r)=r^3-2r^2+4. Straight substitution
and cancellation give

    Q(r):=F-cs
      =(r+2)^3(r^4-4r^3+7r^2-6r+4)
        /[4(r^2+2)^2 h(r)].                            (14)

The denominator is positive on [0,2]: the minimum of h occurs at 4/3
and is 76/27. Define the polynomials

    L(r)=-11r^7+86r^6-188r^5+44r^4+212r^3-88r^2+80,
    U(r)= 21r^7-106r^6+228r^5-84r^4-172r^3+168r^2+80.

Then

    Q(r)-27/64=L(r)/[64(r^2+2)^2 h(r)],
    37/64-Q(r)=U(r)/[64(r^2+2)^2 h(r)].                 (15)

Both polynomials are strictly positive on [0,2]. Here is a complete
finite coefficient certificate. For t=r/2 write

    P(r)=sum_(j=0)^7 c_j binom(7,j)t^j(1-t)^(7-j).

The coefficients, obtained simply by expanding the displayed identity,
are as follows:

| j | L coefficient | U coefficient |
|---|---:|---:|
| 0 | 80 | 80 |
| 1 | 80 | 80 |
| 2 | 1328/21 | 112 |
| 3 | 2736/35 | 4784/35 |
| 4 | 6768/35 | 2672/35 |
| 5 | 4432/21 | 1136/7 |
| 6 | 1168/7 | 2192/7 |
| 7 | 208 | 1232 |

All coefficients are strictly positive, and the Bernstein basis on
[0,1] is nonnegative and sums to one. Equations (14)--(15) therefore prove

    27/64<Q(r)<37/64                                   (16)

for every allowed quadrilateral section. This is an algebraic proof,
not an inference from sampled values. Reversing the plane preserves the
same strict two-sided bound.

## 7. Completion and equality

If a<=3/8, the single correction c in (3) works for every vertex section
by Section 3 and every quadrilateral section by Sections 4--6. These
exhaust proper section polygons of a tetrahedron. A plane containing a
vertex or edge gives a triangular section already included in Section 3;
a genuine quadrilateral has strict two-versus-two vertex signs.
Weighted summation of (2) and the exact scalar balance proves (1).

If a>3/8, Section 5 excludes all quadrilateral sections. Since a>1/3,
only the section isolating v_0 can be vertex-isolating with centroid y.
All remaining sections are its two orientations. Their areas agree,
and positive vector balance makes their total weights equal. Their
mean cap fraction is 1/2, which is strictly greater than 27/64.

Finally equality in the first case allows no quadrilateral cap by (16),
no complemented vertex cap by Section 3, and forces b=1/4 by (6).
Thus a=1/4. Its vertex margins are 4xi_j-1, their cap fractions are
27/64, and their section-normal vectors are a common positive factor
times grad xi_j. The only relation among these four barycentric
covectors is a multiple of their sum zero. The aggregated normalized
weights are consequently all 1/4. Conversely those four weighted caps
meet every hypothesis and attain equality. This proves the full stated
classification.
